approach.summary: A centre-left government running mixed policy: a rules-based fiscal framework (looser than the 2016 spending cap it replaced) and an independent, inflation-targeting central bank, alongside a large role for directed credit and redistributive spending and tax measures.

policies.name: Fiscal framework (spending corridor and primary target)
policies.why: Rules-based: real federal spending growth is held between 0.6% and 2.5% a year and tied to revenue and to an annual primary-balance target with a 0.25-point tolerance band. Looser than the zero-real-growth cap of 2016 that it replaced, and the Senate's fiscal institution doubts the 2027 target can be met without freezing spending.

sources.label: IMF, Brazil: 2025 Article IV Consultation, staff report (IMF Country Report, 17 July 2025)
IFI (Brazilian Senate), Relatório de Acompanhamento Fiscal nº 116

policies.name: Monetary policy (Banco Central do Brasil, inflation targeting)
policies.why: Orthodox: the central bank answered inflation expectations rising above the target band with a tightening cycle from September 2024, 450 basis points of hikes to 15% by June 2025; the Selic target has since been cut (see the stored series for today's level).

sources.label: IMF, Brazil: 2025 Article IV Consultation, staff report (IMF Country Report, 17 July 2025)
Banco Central do Brasil, SGS series 432 (Selic target), stored as br.selic.target

policies.name: Directed (earmarked) credit through state banks and BNDES
policies.why: Interventionist: credit at regulated or subsidised rates is a large share of lending (42.2% in January 2025 by the IMF's count, below its 2016-17 peak of half), and the IMF estimates that policy-rate changes pass through to it at only about a fifth of the rate seen in market lending.

sources.label: IMF, Brazil: 2025 Article IV Consultation, staff report (IMF Country Report, 17 July 2025)

policies.name: Minimum wage, benefits and income-tax changes
policies.why: Redistributive: benefits and pensions are linked to the minimum wage (its real growth is now capped at 2.5% a year), and an income-tax reform adds a minimum tax of up to 10% for individuals earning over R$50,000 a month.

sources.label: IMF, Brazil: 2025 Article IV Consultation, staff report (IMF Country Report, 17 July 2025)

policies.name: Consumption-tax reform (dual VAT, CBS and IBS)
policies.why: Efficiency-oriented and broadly supported by orthodox economists: Complementary Law 214/2025 replaces several cascading consumption taxes with a dual VAT, phased in from 2027.

sources.label: IMF, Brazil: 2025 Article IV Consultation, staff report (IMF Country Report, 17 July 2025)

episodes.name: Collor Plan
episodes.summary: A shock plan on the new president's first full day: 80% of private financial assets were frozen for 18 months, wages and prices were temporarily frozen, the cruzeiro replaced the cruzado novo, and the exchange rate was floated. Inflation was not durably beaten: a second Collor plan followed, then the Marcílio plan from May 1991.

against.why: A drastic squeeze on liquid money did not end inflation for long. Brazilian economists read this as inertial inflation driven by indexation, which a money squeeze alone does not break.

episodes.name: Real Plan
episodes.summary: A plan that treated inflation as both a fiscal problem and an inertial one: a non-monetary unit of account (the URV, worth about one US dollar) let prices realign before the real replaced it on 1 July 1994. The real was kept close to the dollar and depreciated gradually until the maxi-devaluation of the January 1999 crisis. Hyperinflation ended.

against.why: Ending years of high inflation took fiscal correction and a nominal anchor, the reverse of the view that a currency issuer's deficits matter only once real resources run out.

episodes.name: Tequila crisis
episodes.summary: After a rebellion in Chiapas and the assassination of a presidential candidate in 1994, reserves ran low and the government had issued dollar-linked short-term bills (tesobonos). On 20 December 1994 the new government devalued; two days later the peso floated and kept falling. A US-led rescue followed; 1995 brought recession and high inflation, then recovery under a floating peso.

against.why: Years of liberalisation, privatisation and trade opening (NAFTA in 1994) did not prevent a balance-of-payments crisis.
A large official rescue was followed by recovery rather than a prolonged liquidation.

regional.name: Convertibility (currency board)
regional.summary: The peso was pegged one-to-one to the US dollar with full convertibility, to end hyperinflation, along with mass privatisation and deregulation. It worked at first; the regime ended in the 2001–02 collapse, with default and frozen bank deposits (the corralito).

against.why: Giving up discretionary money creation altogether was followed by the end of hyperinflation.

regional.name: Exchange controls (cepo)
regional.summary: Restrictions on buying US dollars from 2011, with a parallel ("blue") dollar trading well above the official rate, until the controls were lifted at the start of Mauricio Macri's presidency in 2015.

against.why: Sustaining demand behind exchange controls was followed by stagnation rather than recovery (see what followed).

regional.name: Fernández government
regional.summary: Exchange controls, reintroduced in late 2019, were tightened; the IMF programme was replaced by a new Extended Fund Facility in 2022. Inflation rose to 100% (the highest since 1991) and reached 211.4% for 2023 by INDEC's count.

against.why: Spending by a currency issuer with large dollar debts and little credibility was followed by spiralling inflation, the constraint MMT itself places on countries without full monetary sovereignty.

regional.name: Milei shock therapy
regional.summary: A 104% devaluation of the official peso, then a 2% monthly crawl, and spending cuts that delivered the first budget surplus since 2011. Monthly inflation fell from 25.5% in December 2023 to 8.8% in April 2024; activity cooled.

against.why: A sharp fiscal contraction was followed by rapid disinflation; see what followed for growth.
